$comment: Frozen escaping vectors for the JSON access log (freeunit-exp issue 70). Data, not prose: a test reads this file and asserts own/expect/jlen per vector. Byte strings use \\xNN for every byte outside printable ASCII (0x20-0x7E) or where the byte is a backslash or quote. Measured against master b09815f1: nxt_conf_json_escape() (src/nxt_conf.c:2745) escapes quote, backslash and every byte <= 0x1F, and copies every other byte unchanged; nxt_utf8_sanitize() (src/nxt_utf8.c:199) replaces each byte that begins no valid UTF-8 sequence with U+FFFD before the writer sees it (src/nxt_router_access_log.c:353).

notation.own: sink=access-log value after nxt_utf8_sanitize() and before escaping; writer=the escaped bytes appended to the record buffer
notation.expect: the exact bytes the writer must append for the bytes of own
notation.jlen: nxt_conf_json_escape_length() for those bytes: the length of expect in bytes
notation.hex: \u00XX uses UPPERCASE hex digits, as nxt_conf.c:2790 writes them

rules.rule: One JSON text, one line: a record is a single escaped JSON object followed by exactly one \n. No value may contain a raw byte below 0x20, a raw quote or a raw backslash, so no value can move the record boundary. This is what closes the #376 forged-line class in the JSON path.

The escaped output is valid UTF-8 because the sink guarantees a valid UTF-8 input: the escaping layer neither validates nor repairs UTF-8. Every invalid sequence is replaced with U+FFFD (EF BF BD) by nxt_utf8_sanitize() before the writer runs. RFC 8259 Sect. 8.1 requires JSON text to be UTF-8.

U+FFFD is the replacement for every invalid byte, one U+FFFD per invalid input byte, not one per maximal subpart. Worst-case expansion is therefore three output bytes per input byte and a declared record bound must be computed after sanitisation, not before.
'/' is not escaped. RFC 8259 does not require it and escaping it only breaks naive substring consumers.
rules.evidence: src/nxt_conf.c:2745-2760: the only escaped bytes are '\\', '"' and <= 0x1F

rules.rule: DEL (0x7F) is copied raw. It is not a JSON metacharacter and it is identical in UTF-8.

The writer does not own the sink-to-writer contract: a caller that hands raw bytes to the escaper is out of contract, and no row here excuses it. The only sanctioned producer of writer input is the sink after nxt_utf8_sanitize().

U+2028 and U+2029 are copied unchanged. RFC 8259 allows them unescaped and JSON.parse has accepted them since ES2019; only a consumer that embeds a record in a JavaScript script is affected, and that consumer should parse the line rather than eval it. If the maintainer decides to escape them anyway, the writer gains a three-byte lookahead and these three rows change with it.
rules.evidence: RFC 8259 Sect. 7 (unescaped = %x20-21 / %x23-5B / %x5D-10FFFF); the decision is recorded, not enforced

rules.rule: request_time: the name and the shape travel together, and a record carries one of them, never both. See numeric_field_shapes.

vectors.why: the ordinary row: nothing is escaped and the copy is bulk
a quote ends the JSON string; unescaped it forges a field boundary (#376 class)
a backslash starts an escape sequence; unescaped it changes the decoding of the next byte
the classic CVE-shaped pair: a backslash before a quote must not let the quote through
R4: the forward slash stays as it is, so a consumer can match a path by substring
the five control bytes that have short JSON escapes; the writer must prefer the short form
every other byte below 0x20 is \u00XX, including NUL
the lowest escape the long form covers
vertical tab has no short JSON escape, so it takes the long form
the highest byte the long form covers; uppercase hex is visible in the B
R5: 0x7F is above the escape threshold and is copied unchanged
a valid multi-byte sequence is copied byte for byte
the astral plane, four bytes, copied unchanged by the writer

U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR is valid JSON text and is copied unchanged. It is a line terminator in JavaScript source, so a consumer that embeds a record in a script (rather than parsing it) sees a break that JSON itself does not have. Escaping it is a client-hardening decision, not a JSON requirement: the row pins the bytes so the decision is testable either way.
U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR, same class as U+2028.
The separators inside a value with ASCII around them, so a writer that starts escaping them must escape these and nothing else.
sink: one U+FFFD for the lone lead byte; the writer then copies the three U+FFFD bytes unchanged
sink: per-byte replacement, so a truncated four-byte sequence becomes up to four U+FFFD; R3
sink: 0x80 starts no sequence on its own
sink: U+D800 encoded as ED A0 80 is refused by the decoder, so three raw bytes become three U+FFFD
sink: C0 80 is an overlong NUL and is refused; 0xC0 itself is refused by nxt_utf8_decode2, so both bytes are replaced
#377 case: a raw 0x80-0xFF byte in a request target reaches the sink and leaves as U+FFFD, never raw
the three cases in one value: a copy run, a sink replacement and a writer escape
the empty value is a legal JSON string
#376 as a vector: CR LF inside the target, plus a forged 'FAKE: LINE' header. The escaped form contains no raw CR, LF or quote, so the record stays one line
vectors.note: this vector is the percent-decoded target BEFORE escaping only if the variable handler hands back raw bytes; the handler for $request_line does percent-decode, so the bytes that reach the sink are 0x0D 0x0A. Use forged-line-decoded for the byte level; this row pins that a literal percent-encoded target is not double-decoded by the writer.

vectors.why: #376 byte level: the decoded CR and LF must come out as \r and \n, so no consumer can see two records

R6 negative vector: this is raw invalid UTF-8, the writer is not allowed to be handed it, and the row exists to catch a caller that skips the sink. The bytes 0xC3 0x28 are not a valid sequence; if a test ever feeds this to the writer directly, the sink contract has been broken and the test must fail rather than accept a record.

numeric_field_shapes.why: request_time is the one field with a type decision behind it. Both candidate shapes are representable in nxt_conf_value_t today, and the choice changes what a consumer reads, so both are frozen here as data, not as prose.
numeric_field_shapes.source_fact: nxt_http_var_request_time() computes integer milliseconds (ms = (now - start_time) / 1000000) and prints seconds with three decimals via %T.%03M, so the integer shape loses nothing against the source and both shapes are exact for every value the text form can print.

shapes.name: integer-milliseconds
shapes.breaks: anything that read the old text field as seconds; a bare 41 in a field named request_time is the silent case, which is why the unit belongs in the name

shapes.name: decimal-seconds
shapes.mechanism: NXT_CONF_VALUE_NUMBER prints its stored text verbatim (src/nxt_conf.c:2442-2444), but there is no public setter: the parser is the only producer (src/nxt_conf.c:2330-2336)
shapes.breaks: nothing, if the name and the fraction stay; it is what the text format already prints, so an existing consumer keeps working

numeric_field_shapes.rule: Freeze exactly one. A record must never carry both, and the field name must match the shape: request_time_ms is an integer, request_time is decimal seconds. A test that accepts either shape accepts the ambiguity the name exists to remove.
numeric_field_shapes.measured_on: o-build (aarch64 Alpine, gcc 15.2.0), against build/lib/libnxt.a from the tree configured at 08c3b866

measured_result.method: exp/request_time_shapes.c built against build/lib/libnxt.a; the integer shape via nxt_conf_set_member_integer(), the decimal shape via nxt_conf_json_parse() on the exact text the format prints
findings: Both shapes are valid JSON numbers and the parser accepts every value measured, including 3600.000; no length limit bites at these widths (NXT_CONF_MAX_NUMBER_LEN is 14).
The decimal shape reproduces the digits the current format already prints, so an existing consumer that treats the field as seconds keeps working; it must parse a number rather than a string.
The integer shape is the same instant named differently: 41 against 0.041. A consumer that assumed seconds reads 41 seconds, which is why the unit belongs in the field name.
NXT_CONF_VALUE_INTEGER has a public setter (nxt_conf_set_member_integer); NXT_CONF_VALUE_NUMBER has none, so the decimal shape needs a new setter while the integer shape does not.
